analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal statutory right to obtain and provide contraception, overriding state restrictions.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 51-39 to advance the bill, but it needed 60 votes, so the bill died without ever being debated or amended in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Right to Contraception Act would write into federal law the right of any person to obtain and use contraception and the right of doctors, nurses, and pharmacists to provide it. It would override any federal or state law that restricts contraception—even laws passed before or after enactment—and would let patients and providers sue in federal court to strike down such restrictions, with the government bearing attorney's fees if it loses. It would apply even over the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and would not change health insurance coverage rules. It died in the Senate when a vote to begin debate failed 51-39, short of the 60 votes needed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use or may use contraception—particularly women of reproductive age—would gain a federally enforceable right to obtain it even in states that restrict it, and health care providers would gain legal protection for providing it. The bill would also help low-income patients in states where local restrictions make contraception harder to get.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who use contraception, and their providers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a statutory right for individuals to obtain contraceptives and engage in contraception, free from coercion.
Prohibits federal and state governments from enforcing any law that restricts the sale, provision, or use of contraception, superseding conflicting state law.
Gives patients and providers a private right of action to sue government officials who enforce restrictions, with attorney's fees for prevailing plaintiffs and abrogation of state sovereign immunity.
Overrides the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as applied to contraception access, so religious-exemption claims cannot be used to block contraceptive care.

analysis.who_pays: Governments that restrict contraception would lose that power and face lawsuits; opponents also argued it overrides state authority and religious-liberty protections. Insurers' coverage obligations are unchanged.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state laws and applies notwithstanding the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which critics argue tramples religious-liberty protections for institutions and individuals with moral objections to contraception.

It preempts federal and state law with a low bar for challenging restrictions—defendants must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a rule significantly advances access—a sweeping transfer of authority from states to federal courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits for ordinary people—a guaranteed legal right to contraception enforceable against state restrictions—are substantial, and it includes an exception allowing restrictions proven necessary by clear and convincing evidence. Its costs are the preemption of state law in this area, override of RFRA in this context, and litigation exposure for governments. On balance it is a straightforward civil-rights protection whose cost falls on governments seeking to restrict contraception, not on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate failed a procedural vote that needed 60 senators just to start debating the bill, and Majority Leader Schumer then withdrew it from consideration by voice vote.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on May 21, 2024, and it was placed directly on the Senate calendar—skipping committee—so it could get a floor vote.
On June 5, 2024, the Senate held a cloture vote on the motion to proceed, the vote required just to begin debating the bill.
Cloture failed 51-39, short of the 60 votes needed; 38 of 40 Republicans voted no, while 46 Democrats, 3 independents, and 2 Republicans (Collins and Murkowski) voted yes.
After the failed vote, the Senate agreed by voice vote to table the motion to proceed, and no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that want to restrict contraception, and the senators who voted no, benefit because no federal right to contraception was created.

for.name: Senator Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Right to Contraception Act and led the effort to bring it to the Senate floor.

for.name: Senator Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Made the motion to proceed and filed cloture to bring the bill up for a vote.

for.name: 49 Democratic and independent senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (50 total sponsors and cosponsors) and voted to advance it.

for.name: Senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Voted with Democrats to advance the bill—the only two Republicans to do so.

against.name: 38 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture on the motion to proceed, denying the bill the 60-vote supermajority needed to begin debate.

against.name: Senator Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: After the failed cloture vote, moved to table the motion to proceed, withdrawing the bill from consideration by voice vote.

sides.party_line_note: The vote to advance the bill split almost entirely by party: 49 of 50 Democrats and independents voted yes, while 38 of 40 Republicans voted no; only Republicans Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski crossed over.

industries.note: The bill protects access to FDA-approved contraceptive drugs, devices, and biologics, guaranteeing a protected market channel; it does not regulate their price or restrict the industry.

industries.industry: State governments seeking to restrict contraception
industries.note: States would lose the power to restrict contraception and be subject to suit by the Attorney General or private plaintiffs, with attorney's fees awarded against them.
Providers gain an explicit statutory right to provide contraception and related information, plus standing to sue on behalf of their patients.
